drapeaux.note: Oath formula copied word for word from Blackstone, Commentaries, Book III, ch. 22 (Avalon Project, Yale, and Lonang texts, both read): "hear this, ye justices, that I do not own unto Richard Jones the sum of ten pounds, nor any penny thereof, in manner and form as the said Richard has declared against me. So help me God." The word is "own" (archaic for "owe") in the source. The French entry's source note (url avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/blackstone_bk3ch22.asp) matches.

Section XIII of the Civil Procedure Act 1833 (3 & 4 Will. IV, c. 42), read at the Irish Statute Book URL: "And be it further enacted, That no Wager of Law shall be hereafter allowed." The quoted phrase is verbatim; the page dates the Act [14th August 1833].

titre: Wager of law: eleven neighbors to swear you owe nothing
accroche: In England, a debtor could escape a debt by swearing, with eleven neighbors, that he owed nothing. Parliament abolishes this proof on August 14, 1833.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Blackstone's example, a certain Richard Jones claims ten pounds from a defendant before an English court. The defendant does not want to pay, or swears he owes nothing. The procedure of *wager of law* opens a third way for him: no proof, no witnesses, no argument on the merits, but an oath.

## Twelve oaths for one debt

The jurist William Blackstone, in his *Commentaries on the Laws of England* in the 18th century, describes how a defendant makes his law. The defendant first undertakes, by giving security, to appear on a fixed day. On that day, he comes with eleven of his neighbors. The judges warn him of the gravity of a false oath. If he persists, he swears, in Blackstone's words: “hear this, ye justices, that I do not own unto Richard Jones the sum of ten pounds, nor any penny thereof, in manner and form as the said Richard has declared against me. So help me God.”

Then the eleven neighbors swear that they believe, in conscience, that he speaks the truth. Blackstone notes the difference: he swears on his faith, they on their belief. None of them says he saw anything. The defendant walks out free, forever discharged of the debt. Blackstone follows Coke on the number: such a proof is equivalent to a verdict for the defendant, and so it needs the same number of voices as a jury, twelve.

## Why people believed in it

The reason lies, Blackstone writes, in the ancient Saxon constitution: each man's credit before the courts depended on the opinion his neighbors had of his truthfulness. The ancestors also held that an innocent man of good reputation could be crushed by a multitude of false witnesses: the defendant's oath was a bulwark.

English law itself distrusted it. Blackstone observes that it allows it only in very few cases, and that it provided other remedies in which the defendant is excluded from it. According to Wikipedia, *assumpsit*, an action based on the promise the debtor is presumed to have made, did not admit wager of law, and creditors used it more and more to recover their debts.

## The end, in 1833

Trial by battle (*wager of battle*) is abolished in 1819. Wager of law outlives it by fourteen years. According to Wikipedia, a clergyman in Staffordshire was still using it in 1829 against an ironmonger of Stafford who was claiming money from him: he and his co-swearers, moreover, did not show up on the appointed date.

The British Parliament ends it with the *Civil Procedure Act 1833*, a law reforming procedure, whose Article XIII, given royal assent on August 14, 1833, fits on a single line: “no Wager of Law shall be hereafter allowed.” It does not say why. It merely removes a proof that rested on no fact, only on what neighbors said they believed of a man's word.

In a jury, twelve people also swear an oath. The difference lies in what they are asked to do: judge an account they did not live through, or vouch for a man they know.

repere.texte: On August 14, 1833, Article XIII of the Civil Procedure Act (3 & 4 Will. IV, c. 42) of the British Parliament provides that “no Wager of Law shall be hereafter allowed”: a debtor can no longer escape a debt by swearing, with eleven neighbors who swear they believe him.
repere.source: Civil Procedure Act 1833, 3 & 4 Will. IV, c. 42, Article XIII, text published by the Irish Statute Book

carte.punch: Swearing you owe nothing, with eleven neighbors as guarantors: an English proof until 1833.
carte.idee: In an English court, a defendant could dismiss a debt by swearing he owed nothing, with eleven neighbors swearing they believed him: twelve oaths were worth a verdict. Parliament abolished this wager of law on August 14, 1833.

quiz.question: What do the eleven neighbors who accompany the defendant swear in a wager of law?
choix: That they believe in conscience that the defendant is telling the truth
That they themselves witnessed the repayment of the debt
That they will pay the debt in his place if the defendant lies
That they know the creditor and consider him a liar
quiz.explication: Blackstone distinguishes the defendant's oath, who swears on his faith, from that of the eleven neighbors, who swear only on their belief: they attest to no fact. None says he saw the payment, none commits his own money, and none accuses the creditor.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When was wager of law abolished in England, and by what text?
choix: On August 14, 1833, by a ruling of the House of Lords
In 1819, by the same text that abolishes trial by battle
On August 14, 1833, by Article XIII of the Civil Procedure Act
In 1829, after the case of the Staffordshire clergyman
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Civil Procedure Act 1833 is an Act of Parliament, not a court decision. Its Article XIII, given royal assent on August 14, 1833, abolishes wager of law fourteen years after the abolition of trial by battle, by a separate text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What reason does Blackstone give to justify the old trust in wager of law?
choix: Saxon courts admitted no form of proof other than the collective oath
The king required every debt to be proven by a number of witnesses equal to its amount in pounds
The Church forbade any other mode of proof in disputes between individuals
In the ancient Saxon constitution, each man's credit depended on his neighbors' opinion of his truthfulness
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Blackstone ties the practice to the ancient Saxon constitution: a man's word was worth what his neighbors said of it. English law, moreover, provided other remedies in which the defendant could not resort to the oath.
